description: For this hackathon, I’m particularly interested in challenges involving satellite imagery, Earth observation, change detection, anomaly detection, and astronomical data. Our team is already complete, so we are not currently looking for additional members.
summary: FireTrace Explorer lets anyone investigate the 2026 Plaskett Fire (Big Sur, California) through NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band radar, which sees through the smoke that blinds optical satellites. Our offline, reproducible pipeline compares NISAR GCOV HH/HV images from 16 August and 3 October 2026, computes a continuous change index (|ΔHH| + |ΔHV|, robust z-score) on a 10 m grid, and sets it beside the official WFIGS fire perimeter. The web app shows the before/after radar, the observed changes, a guided 3D story and an Evidence Inspector that reports the real values, method and cautions (steep slope, radar layover/shadow, perimeter edge, rainfall) for any pixel. Of the 1,050 ha of highlighted radar change, 99.96 % lies inside the 12,135 ha perimeter. We are explicit about uncertainty: observed radar change is not confirmed burned area or severity.
details:
FireTrace Explorer turns satellite radar measurements into an interactive, transparent exploration of landscape change. Our prototype focuses on the 2026 Plaskett Fire in Big Sur, California, comparing NASA–ISRO NISAR observations from August 16 and October 3.

We process NISAR L2 GCOV radar data offline, comparing before-and-after backscatter in HH and HV polarizations on a common 10-meter analysis grid. The application displays continuous radar changes alongside a dated official fire perimeter. Users can compare observations, explore layers, and inspect numerical evidence at individual locations or along a transect. Sentinel-2 imagery, terrain and precipitation provide complementary context.

Our intended impact is to make complex radar observations accessible to students, researchers and people interested in wildfire landscapes. Rather than presenting an unexplained detection map, FireTrace connects visual patterns to measurements, methods, sources and limitations.

We developed the processing pipeline in Python using NumPy, rasterio and geospatial libraries, the API with FastAPI, and the web application with React, TypeScript, Vite and MapLibre GL JS. Precomputed products keep heavy processing outside the interactive experience.

The project's creative contribution is its evidence-first approach: combining an interactive map, guided storytelling and an Evidence Inspector while explicitly separating observation from interpretation. Our team considered reproducibility, invalid-data handling, spatial alignment, accessibility, data provenance and environmental factors that can affect radar signals.

FireTrace is a working research and educational prototype, not an operational wildfire alert system or a validated burned-area classifier. Radar changes may also reflect moisture, terrain, vegetation or acquisition geometry. The reference perimeter predates the second observation and is not pixel-level ground truth.
